As with many other similar apps, I played til my initial allotment of credits ran out (didn't take long) and then I deleted the app.

The game is fun to play but, like so many others, to really keep playing you need to use real money to purchase coins/credits. You don't HAVE to but you'll likely be waiting for the four hour waiting period to expire before which you can't receive more credits/coins and continue playing (for free).

The game does have good graphics and sound as well as many different slot machines to play with different themes. However, unless you happen to do very well, you'll likely be checking for and collecting your bonus credits every so often and using them up rather quickly only to wait for more. As with most of these games, I wish they would simply charge a fair price for them and let you continue to play (setting your own initial starting bank-roll) and to simply start over if you run out. This would be preferable to trying to nickel and dime you to death every time you run out of credits/coins.

I find myself playing it for only a few minutes until I quickly run out of my small amount of credits. This gets tiresome quickly and I'll likely end up deleting the game and searching for something that allows me to play for a longer period of time thus having more fun.

To game developers: Please charge a set price for your games and do away with the constant need to keep paying more and more to continue playing these games as we go along. Many times I'll simply stop and delete a game once I see that it employs this method of requiring more and more money beyond the purchase price (whether it's a free or a paid app).

I've now had a chance to play with the app and I really like it. In fact, I liked it so much I played through all 17 levels plus the bonus level in one sitting. You have a couple of different choices for how to control the helicopter. I chose the "tilt control" option which is indicated as being "a bit difficult) but I picked it right off the bat and it seemed so intuitive that I didn't bother trying the other control options.

You go through each level where you are given a different challenge to complete. There are three different criteria that must be met on each level and if you complete all three criteria you receive a star for each one (similar system used in other games/apps). If you receive less than three stars on a level you can choose to repeat the level as many times as you wish or simply move on to the next level. There are some levels where you get to fire tracer rounds or missiles to help complete the level. Or, in some cases, chose NOT to use them to complete the level. I only wish there had been even more levels. The graphics are somewhat plain but detailed and there are limited sound effects. However, for me, controlling the helicopter and the challenge of trying to get all three stars on each level was enough to keep me entertained. I found the app fun and enjoyed the many different challenges each new level provided.

Now that the developer has removed some questionable code and I've had a chance to play around with the app, I'm happy to have raised my rating on this app up to 5 stars and I don't very often rate apps at 5 stars.

I will agree with the other posts in that there are no instructions or anything to show you how the 'game' works or even what the goal is and that this would have been helpful. However, I don't quite understand the people that are so vehemently trashing the app for that reason alone saying it is horrible and impossible to figure out, etc. Granted, the first few times I played it I wasn't quite sure what to do. However after pressing the ">>" button to get started you find with a very little bit of trial and error that one figures out that by sliding your finger around on the screen that you can rotate the position of the colored geometric shape that the white shape is flying towards allowing the white shape to "fly into" an open side of the colored geometric shape. Once inside, one finds yet another colored geometric shape you must twist and turn to make the white geometric shape fly into and so on and so on. You continue doing this until such time as you don't quite fly the white shape into the colored shape but instead you crash into the wall thus ending that run. Then after a quick bit of showing you the path the white shape took but in reverse, you are ready to start again by press in the ">>" key again. There really isn't a whole lot to the game but it is something that at first seems rather difficult but after trying it several time you gradually get the hang of it and you are able to clear more and more shapes/rounds/levels or whatever you want to call them. As I said it's quite simple and the drive to do just a "little bit" better each time is what keeps you coming back to play this very simple but challenging game. There's a decent little sound track and the graphics while basic are pretty good.

The game uses Game Circle if you choose to turn it on and shows a leader board with your overall rank. There are various achievements you can attain such as so many levels completed etc.

About the only gripe I had with the game was that after you finish a round and finally crash into one of the shapes it often takes way to long for the game to reset so you can try again. Once you crash, the game sort of plays back the route you took by showing you a reverse animation of your path. Granted it's greatly accelerated but it still takes a few seconds that was (at least I thought) unnecessary. I found myself wanting to jump right back in and try it again as quick as possible and not have to wait for this silly animation to replay in reverse before I could get started.

I ended up enjoying the app. It's something you can play when you have a few moments to spare. While very daunting at first, I found by the end of the first day I had made it up to a personal best of 30 levels/rounds. A number that when I first started I certainly thought would have been impossible given I was struggling to get more than two or three levels.

The app was certainly worth getting as a Free App of the Day.

I've edited this review a few times to include additional information. One of the most important things people need to know is about how the quests/tasks are started. I learned this lesson the hard way so I'm hoping this tip will help some other people avoid the mistake I made. You will realize early on that you need money/cash in this game to buy land, buildings and other things. You earn certain amounts of money by doing certain things and by getting revenue from the houses and things you build. You will be tempted to keep sending your characters on short quests to earn money. You might be tempted (like I was) to always keep your characters busying earning money. Don't do this. Why, well the reason being is that the different characters have to be available (not on quests) in order to receive new and important quest lines from the game. If you characters are busy you will earn money and you will level up but you will miss out on starting a good number of the important quests along the way at the point that you normally should. Quests that unlock various buildings or various characters in the game at certain points but they can't be given to your various characters if they are busy doing some other task. I'm now further along in the game and I've found by keeping my characters busy all the time doing 1/2 hour, 1 hour, 2 hour quests, I haven't gotten quests I should have gotten at much lower levels. Now, I'm assuming that the quests will still come but if I had it to do over I would for sure not keep my characters busy all the time trying to earn a few dollars here and there. You can build and farm some houses if you want to build up some cash but don't keep your characters busy all the time with the basic quests that are always available. Wait for the new ones to come in as they need to. If you do some of the other shorter quests that are available all the time make sure you to at least let your character(s) sit around for a while not doing anything before you send them on a quest. You will start to see the dialogue boxes that pop up where characters are talking to each other. Those are typically where/when the quests are given out. Make sure your characters sit around and wait for a while to see if any of those are popping. If a character is busy on a quest those dialogue boxes won't/can't come up. I'm still waiting for quests from MUCH lower levels to show up and not even sure if they will. I've read you can put certain things like certain houses into storage and then bring them back out and that will prompt the system to start a missed quest.

Another quick tip is when you first start the game/app you need to place the first house. There is a shaded square where the house obviously goes. There is a check mark to confirm that's where you want to put the house. Simply tapping the check mark gets you an error message. You need to drag the house down to the shaded square before clicking on the check mark to confirm. That tripped me up for a minute or two so I wanted to mention it to people. Ok, that said, I've played the game a bit now and it's gotten progressively more interesting. It is your typical SIM type game where you have to build a town and choose where to put various buildings, roads, rivers, and can instruct various people in doing certain tasks. There's a lot of waiting involved for time to pass for things to happen. If you have unlimited financial resources you can cause things to happen at a much accelerated rate. But, for the average person/player there is going to be a lot of making some choices and waiting. One frustration I have found with the game so far is it seems to be glitchy, at least on my Kindle Fire HDX 8.9. I found that many times when I go to open the program it will load to the splash screen and then almost immediately close. My device is usually online so it's not a case of needing to get to the network/internet and not being able to. Also, while playing the game it will randomly just shut down. I'll have to reopen it and sometimes have to go through opening it several times because it wants to close right away again. Also today I was playing it and I had just gone into the game after being away from it for several hours so of course there was a lot of collecting of money and XP for things that had gone on or finished while I was away from the game. After I had seen to that I clicked on the Barbarian Castle and saw that I had the option to Get Revenge for my building(s) being damaged while I was away. I chose the Revenge option but nothing happened. I clicked on it several more times after waiting a moment or to but again nothing happened. I even chose another unrelated option in between but nothing happened. The Revenge option was there and it was red but for some reason just wouldn't work. These little glitches of the game not loading or suddenly shutting down or now having options that suddenly don't work are getting annoying.

Some further thoughts on the game...
One of the items in the game that I think could be handled better I think is the system whereby you acquire and use "Donuts". Donuts are type of currency in the game in that if you have them you can use them to purchase/acquire things or make things happen faster (accelerate a task like making a building's construction period go faster for example). Donuts are a very precious commodity in the game but are hard to come by. I understand this was done on purpose as the goal of the game is to try and get you to spend additional (real) money on the game by purchasing Donuts with real money. Something I abhor doing in these games. I wish developers would simply charge what they need to for a game and give you the "Complete" game. Instead, they give you the game for free or $.99 and then try and nickel and dime you to death with buying add-on, upgrades or things you pretty much have to have to continue or advance in the game. It's very annoying but it is so ingrained in the App culture now that you pretty much can't get away from it in most cases. To find a game/app that you can play and enjoy for a significant length of time without having to spend additional (real) money on the game is very rare. Anyway, with regards to donuts they are very hard to come by in the game but can be purchased with real money. One thing I think they should do is make acquiring donuts much easier. I know this cuts into their bottom line but it would make the game so much more enjoyable. Also, I found out (to late) that there is an option that you can tuArn on that confirms when you are spending/using donuts for something (for example to buy something in the game) instead of using "in-game" cash. That makes it easier to not spend/use donuts for something unless it's really important. I made the mistake early on where I was trying to add some simple item like a section of fence. I looked and the item was very inexpensive in that it was only $1 of "in game" money...not a big deal so I put up a whole bunch of these sections of fence. Suddenly while placing these sections of fence I got a message that I didn't have enough to place any more fence sections. I thought that was odd since I had plenty of money. In looking closer I suddenly realized that the fence sections I had been placing weren't at a cost of $1 each of "in game" money as I thought but were instead ONE DONUT each. I had wasted about 10 donuts on fencing sections. What a waste. So, my suggestion would be to not only make "donuts" easier to acquire in the game and to make that option where you need to confirm that you are using donuts for some action or purchase, that it be ON by default so you don't learn the hard way you are spending donuts on something as trivial as fencing or something similar. Right now the option is OFF by default and you have to find it and turn it on. You do get some Donuts here and there in the game for things like leveling up (not sure if it's every level...I don't think so). You can also get them at random when having one of the characters to something like clean up garbage or waste in a newly purchased section of land. You can also win some donuts when playing/using some "lottery Scratchers" that you can purchase at the Kwik-E-Mart but the lottery scratch off tickets have to purchased using real money. You can win from one or two Donuts up to I think 100 as the big jackpot. The tickets are $.99 or a $1.00 I believe. There is also at least one (probably more) 'Easter Eggs' where doing a certain task will give you some free donuts. The one I'm referring to has to do with clicking on Homer's task list picture I think it is, a number of times at just the right time and you will get a bunch of free donuts. Just do a search on how to get free "donuts" in the game using a search engine or Youtube and you'll find out step by step what you need to do. The other thing that really irritates me and that I wish they would change about the game is that there are many items including buildings and things that you have to purchase in the game to put into your 'town'. Many of these items or buildings can ONLY be purchased using Donuts, not cash. I think they should either eliminate being able to only purchase items or buildings with Donuts (allow in-game cash purchases for these items) OR make Donuts something that you can purchase in the game using "in-game" money. That way if you didn't want to spend real money but were willing to put the time and effort into say "farming" houses of a particular color, you could get enough "in-game" money to purchase enough Donuts to pretty much do or buy whatever you need throughout the game (eventually).

All in all I'm surprised the game/sim has held my interest as long as it has. I find myself playing it quite a bit. Since I refuse to spend real money for the most part for in-app purchases I've learned very early on that as boring as it is, that I'm going to need to do a fair amount of 'farming' of various color houses to get the in-game cash I need. I don't know if even that is going to be enough when I look at the numerous items that simply require Donuts "only" to purchase. Anyway, IF you are going to farm do it from the very start and set your town up with that in mind. Don't start setting it up in a nice pleasant looking design only to have to rearrange things later to make it more optimal for farming. For farming, I've found simple, large blocks of a particular house color packed in as tight as you can possibly get them to be the most cost effective and quickest way to arrange them. When you come back to your town and want quickly zip through and click on the all those dollar signs to collect all your money and XP points, you aren't going to want to have to bop around to all kinds of little squares of neatly arranged, cute little neighborhoods. It's WAY to time consuming. If farming you'll want to be able to go right down a straight line tapping one dollar sign after another as quick as humanly possible. Even doing that it's a bit of a time consuming chore. One of the several things I wish they would put into the game/sim is when you first launch the game/sim to be able to push a button and in one move collect ALL the money and XP points in one shot so you don't have to go around spending time tapping and tapping and tapping all over the place.

Finally, Game Developers: PLEASE consider making "Donuts" something you can outright purchase with in-game cash. I know for me personally once I reach the point where I can't continue because the buildings or items I need to add to my town simply can't be acquired because the only way to do so is to spend a bunch of "real" money, I'm done. I won't continue once I know I HAVE to start spending a bunch of real money on an app. I'm sure there are a ton of people who are willing to pay out the money (real money) to keep playing and that's fine but I'm not one of them.

Rosetta Stone's method is based on a technique called "Dynamic Immersion." You're immediately thrown into the language you want to learn -- there's no English allowed. This sounds daunting, but the software starts you off at such a rudimentary level it isn't intimidating.

Thankfully, the app employs a good variety of interactive methods (matching pictures to sentences, writing caption for photos, hearing words and phrases pronounced correctly by native speakers, etc.) so the "by rote" factor stays low. Rosetta Stone says its techniques are modeled on how native speakers actually learn their own languages, usually while still kids, and I think that's a good description for what the software delivers. You start with words and then move on to phrases, and then with level two you get to conversations. Level three kicks the conversational up a couple of notches. It's a natural progression.

I really like how the program keeps track of what areas I'm botching and pulls me back into those areas for more work. I also like the pronunciation practice via the included headset, although I can't verify it's always catching me when I'm mispronouncing things. To my ear I'm doing OK, but my ear isn't the best, hence my use of this program. If I'm pronouncing things badly and the program isn't always catching my errors, I'm not sure how I'd know, if you see what I mean. (I'm sure I'll find out once I begin practicing on real people.) My hope is that I can nail the rudiments of Japanese and get a good grip on simple conversations using Rosetta Stone before trying to find people to practice with/on, thus keeping my embarrassment factor low.

I think there are people who prefer a more standard "grammar-first" approach because they've found in the past that this is what works for them. I imagine there are also people who don't like looking at computer screens for lengthy periods. These are valid concerns. There are different pedagogical approaches for a reason -- not everyone learns in the same way. My guess is that Rosetta Stone would serve the majority of people very well, especially students who are comfortable with computer-based learning. Ideally, I think this program will work best for people who are studying a language using many "inputs" (text books, audio programs, computer apps, foreign-language media, Akira Kurosawa flicks, native speakers, etc.) All of these things will ultimately reinforce one another. The more immersion, the better.

Overall, I am very pleased with this product. The program's interface is well-designed, I've experienced no bugs or glitches, and I am making progress faster than I thought I would (or at least I think I am). I'd give the app five stars but I cringe just a little bit at the price. I don't think it is overpriced for what you get, mind you, but the cost -- well, it is what it is. There is a demo on the Rosetta Stone Web site that I encourage you to try before buying. It'll give you a good idea how well this program will work for you. If you like the approach, the price for all three levels is well worth it.

Keep in mind that learning any foreign tongue will realistically take a while, especially Japanese. Rosetta Stone shortens the learning period a good deal and makes sticking with the program easier, but it's only a foundation. Still, it's a pretty darn good one.

CorelDraw Graphics Suite X4 is a very solid program. It does most of what Adobe Illustrator does (vector-based graphic design) and much of what Adobe InDesign does (desktop publishing) in one handy application.

CorelDraw would be an ideal solution for a small business or organization that does a fair amount of advertising-creation and publication design in-house. With one application (well-priced when compared to buying both Illustrator and InDesign), the content creator can achieve very professional results.

The app is also friendly to first-time users. It offers more than 80 customizable document templates that will be useful to newbies. While there is still a learning curve for new users, the app has an intuitive interface that will help get the user up and running relatively quickly.

The problem for CorelDraw is that Illustrator has become the default vector app in the design/pre-press community. Professionals should still start with Illustrator and Quark and/or InDesign -- they're the industry standards. While CorelDraw is very good, it would need to be awesome to unseat Illustrator, and that isn't going to happen anytime soon.

CorelDraw has new file formats that enable docs to be shared between CorelDraw and Adobe apps. This is handy, but also shows which format and apps are the most common -- Adobe's. If you're in a design situation where you're going to have to worry about your files working in Adobe formats, you should just go ahead and use Adobe products.

Another thing: Because the Adobe products are the standard, there are numerous training DVDs and books to purchase that can help you get the most out of your apps. With CorelDraw, not so much.

I feel bad for good apps like CorelDraw. I wish I could talk just about the app itself and not bring in a discussion about Adobe's competitive products, but given the way the design industry works -- or any technology-based industry, for that matter -- you always have to bring the front-running application into the mix.

That being said, if you're not a graphic designer or a pre-press operator but are instead a multitasking, Windows-based employee at a company or organization who has been put in charge of creating brochures, pamphlets and the like, CorelDraw will answer your needs very well. If you're someone who doesn't need to share files often with design colleagues, publishing clients or service bureaus (who are most likely using Adobe apps almost exclusively), then you have no worries.

BTW, if you're already using CoreDraw, it's worth the upgrade. The font-identifying tool alone makes it worth it, at least for me.

I really like how the program keeps track of what areas I'm botching and pulls me back into those areas for more work. I also like the pronunciation practice via the included headset, although I can't verify it's always catching me when I'm mispronouncing things. To my ear I'm doing OK, but my ear isn't the best, hence my use of this program. If I'm pronouncing things badly and the program isn't always catching my errors, I'm not sure how I'd know, if you see what I mean. My hope is that I can nail the rudiments of Italian and get a good grip on simple conversations using Rosetta Stone before trying to find people to practice with/on, thus keeping my embarrassment factor low.

Thankfully, the app employs a good variety of interactive methods (matching pictures to sentences, writing caption for photos, hearing words and phrases pronounced correctly by native speakers, etc.) so the "by rote" factor stays low. Rosetta Stone says its techniques are modeled on how native speakers actually learn their own languages, usually while still kids, and I think that's a good description for what the software delivers. You start with words and then move on to phrases, and then with level two you get to conversations. Level three kicks the conversational up a couple of notches. It's a natural progression.

I think there are people who prefer a more standard "grammar-first" approach because they've found in the past that this is what works for them. I imagine there are also people who don't like looking at computer screens for lengthy periods. These are valid concerns. There are different pedagogical approaches for a reason -- not everyone learns in the same way. My guess is that Rosetta Stone would serve the majority of people very well, especially students who are comfortable with computer-based learning. Ideally, I think this program will work best for people who are studying a language using many "inputs" (text books, audio programs, computer apps, foreign-language media, foreign flicks, native speakers, etc.) All of these things will ultimately reinforce one another. The more immersion, the better.

Overall, I am very pleased with this product. The program's interface is well-designed, I've experienced no bugs or glitches, and I am making progress faster than I thought I would (or at least I think I am). I'd give the app five stars but I cringe just a little bit at the price. I don't think it is overpriced for what you get, mind you, but the cost -- well, it is what it is. There is a demo on the Rosetta Stone Web site that I encourage you to try before buying. It'll give you a good idea how well this program will work for you. If you like the approach, the price for all three levels is well worth it.

Keep in mind that learning any foreign tongue will realistically take a while. Rosetta Stone shortens the learning period a good deal and makes sticking with the program easier, but it's only a foundation. Still, it's a pretty darn good one, and I can see why it's so popular with the international business community.

Disclaimer: I'm not a video-editing expert by any means, and I wasn't looking for something to rival Final Cut. I just needed a piece of software that would allow me to edit video snippets into a professional package for pub quizzes I put together weekly. I also wanted a decent DVD maker that wouldn't choke on mysterious codecs. To that end, I needed something simple and reliable. I didn't need the bells and whistles some might. For my purposes, this app works very well.

It has more of a learning curve than I expected. It has more features than less expensive editing apps I've tried so the interface is more complicated than I needed. But I think most users will like the app's extended functionality. I do wish the instructional booklet were more user-friendly. I had to go online to troubleshoot most of the time.

That being said, once I got my editing method down the app was great for what I needed. The resulting videos are high in quality. The sound features and the transition filters in particular add a professional sheen to my work. And the app outputs and/or converts my video files to many different formats pretty cleanly.

If you've got some v-editing experience under your belt, you'll probably jump right in. In general, I really like Corel apps and I haven't been too disappointed with this one.

This isn't really the app to get solely for driving directions, as there are less-expensive alternatives if you're buying mainly for that purpose. If you need to data-map info from your business or organization, however, than this fits the bill. The GUI isn't elegant, but it gets the job done.

If you're looking for one app suite that will allow you to do basic photo-editing, video-editing and DVD-making, then Corel Digital Studio 2010 isn't a bad choice. The apps included are not top shelf -- they're geared to the amateur user, most of whom will use the apps to perform the same simple tasks over and over (and there's nothing wrong with that -- that's at least 85% of the market). Those users will find this suite a great bargain for the money since the price is much lower than having to buy multiple individual software applications and the results for basic activities are very good.

If you are aiming at doing more advanced work, however, you might consider spending the extra bucks to get Photoshop Elements, Premier Elements, Nero, etc. as standalone apps. They're more powerful than the apps in this suite.

PDF Converter Pro 6 has been hit-or-miss for me. It was hard to install and it sometimes produced PDFs that were just pictures of pages, rather than real PDF conversions. Still, it does some stuff OK. Overall, I'm going to try another PDF converter next time.
After a couple weeks of use, I uninstalled this app. It kept freezing on me while burning DVDs. Never did figure out what was wrong. Maybe it'll work for you.

I've used this for video-editing now for a while. I don't do a lot of video-editing, so I'd like to have an app that is fairly intuitive to use as I don't want to keep having to relearn it. Pro X4 works OK once I get going, but I wish it were easier to jump in and go when you're doing simple stuff. The program interface and the editing process seem like they could be more user-friendly. That said, if you are going to use this app fairly often and therefore find the learning curve a worthwhile investment of your time, you won't be disappointed with the editing quality, given the app's price.

I've been using this to edit clips together into short movies (mainly putting movie clips together for our church's trivia nights) and it's been working fine for that. When I've imported large files, a couple of times I've gotten frozen out.

The interface takes a couple of sessions to get into (for the first couple of weeks, I was Googling instructions often). The DVD writing function has been fine.

Since I don't use this for highly intensive, pro-level film editing, I can't speak to that level of functionality. For the average hobbyist like me, this will probably fit the bill.

I've used PowerDVD since it came installed on my next-to-last computer. It's a solid all-around media player and the Ultra version will play just about anything I can throw at it. It's not all that complicated to learn to use and the TrueTheater technology does a good job with HD upscaling.

Over time, the amount of content I stream has increased and I use PowerDVD less and less. The only reason I still use it, to be honest, is for watching Blur-Ray discs. It handles them well, but if you're not into Blu-Rays, go with a "lower" version of this software (it'll save you bucks) or cobble together a suite of free apps that'll handle all the usual suspects/file types.

I'm disappointed Cyberlink includes "junkware" (additional and useless software) in the install. That's ridiculous. I can see why free apps try to install superfluous software, but an app I've paid for? Please.

PowerDVD 14 Ultra might not seem inexpensive, especially compared to some solid freeware out there. But it's definitely less costly than a home-video component. which I don't need since I have PowerDVD. It's also much more robust than freeware options (it helps that my system is pretty robust, too). In general, I like this app. It has never been buggy and it's a solid and versatile media player.

I've been using Painter since version 4, back when Fractal Design was still behind it. It's always been THE app for artists who want to recreate the look of natural media within the digital space. I was delighted when I received this new version to review.

Over the years, Painter has been moving toward a close compatibility with Photoshop. Not only can you import/export Painter files to Photoshop, but the GUI has also moved from a more idiosyncratic one to one that mirrors the thinking behind PSD. And Painter's natural-media library is so extensive, the app is now beyond compare -- there isn't another app out there that really competes in terms of media replication.

I still use Photoshop and Painter for my digital art. Both apps have their strengths, and Corel has done a great job of ensuring an almost seamless workflow twixt the two apps. Photoshop can be used to make great digital art, especially if you're pretty good with creating brushes, using blend modes and creating texture overlays. But it can't beat Painter for mimicking natural media at a basic "stroke" level. If you want your digital work to look like watercolors, pastels, oils, etc., that have been rendered "by hand," Painter is the tool for you.

By the way, if your art mainly consists of pencil and/or pen work, the much cheaper [[ASIN:B00LH6ZWIG Autodesk SketchBook Pro 7 [Download]]] is a great option for that. I've used and reviewed SketchBook in the past, and it's great for line work and broad color overlays/fill-ins. I don't use SketchBook that often because 1) I already own Painter and it does the line work just as well as SketchBook and 2) Painter's coloring and paint-modeling options are greater than Sketchbook's. But if you don't need the extensive range of natural-media effects Painter offers and you're basically looking for a very good sketch app, keep SketchBook in mind.

BTW, I use a Wacom with Painter and I should mention a tablet greatly aids in the natural media reproduction. That being said, I have used a mouse for Painter and still gotten very good results. But if you get Painter and you're serious about taking advantage of all it can deliver, you'll probably want to invest in a graphics tablet at some point. So figure in the cost of that when you purchase this program. (Even a less-expensive tablet will greatly improve the look of your strokes within the app.)

SUMMARY: Painter is not a cheap app, so if you just need an app that will allow you to create line work and/or very flat artwork, Photoshop and SketchBook will work for you. But if you're an artist looking to recreate natural media to a pretty amazing degree, Painter is worth the money. Nothing else currently available can best this app at what this app sets out to do.

This new version of Dragon NaturallySpeaking adds support for major web-mail programs like Gmail (which is what I use). As with previous versions, you can use it to dictate documents and to orally navigate your computer (including Web browsing).

I haven't used Dragon before, and I found the setup and "training" periods to be longer than I thought. That's not a bad thing, though -- the app is stacked with more functionality than I knew about. I've been using the app for about a week now and I'm still finding out new things it can do. (It's head and shoulders above Windows 7's similar in-house app, which I tried out a couple of years ago to do first drafts of biz docs and later stopped using.)

Before buying the Home version seen here, I'd recommend looking at the features you'd get with the Premium version ([[ASIN:B00LX4BYV6 Dragon NaturallySpeaking Premium 13.0, English]]). For example, if you're a big user of Excel like I am, you might be happier with the Premium version.

I've been using Painter since the 1990s, when it was put out by Fractal Design. It has always been by far the best app in replicating natural media in a digital space. It bills itself as a "paint program," but the dry media included (pastels, chalk, pencil, etc.) are all excellent.

Over the years, Painter's interface and functionality has come to resemble Photoshop, as the two apps are actually very compatible for projects. Still, you'll have to spend some time learning Painter, as it goes pretty deep in both media and workflow customization. If this is your first time using Painter, expect a bit of a learning curve.

If you're not a professional artist or graphic designer and are just looking for an app that does ink and graphite well, you might consider [[ASIN:B00LI95DNG Autodesk SketchBook Pro 7]]. It's less expensive and its simpler drawing/drafting tools are very good. But if you want to do full-fledged digital art -- especially art that mimics trad media even when Giclee-printed -- then invest in Painter. There are only two apps that I can say I actually love top to bottom -- one is Photoshop, the second is Painter. I use one or both of them almost every day.

This is a game requiring mindfulness and strategy. I don't know why I can't get enough of this game, or why it's so addicting. It's the same scenario every time -- different colored buttons "sewn" onto a piece of cloth. You have a few rules, and as you touch the various button groups, they are cut off the cloth by scissors. The goal is to eliminate all the buttons from the cloth as quickly as possible. One would think it would get boring after a while, but for me it never does. I love to challenge myself to do it faster than the one before. I never use sound, but I can just hear the snipping of the scissors in my head every time. There's just something mesmerizing in it for me.

It is very easy when doing Keto, unless you are using a prescribed diet, to find yourself at the end of the day having gone way over your carb count. There are unexpected carbs in a lot of foods, and if you're not tracking them, it's easy to go astray and not to get the results you are looking for without a way to track your foods.

Is it difficult to use? No. Is it time consuming? Yes, in the beginning, it is, but totallyworth it. Luckily, I'm semi-retired so I have more time than a lot of people, but it is so critical for me to lose weight that it is worth it to me to do the cooking and to track the macros. I have a couple of cookbooks that breakdown the macros of each meal, so just entering the macros for those meals is quick. If you have special products that you want to use (which I did), it becomes a little more time consuming because I have to find them (via the app) and enter them manually or by scanning (which you have access to if you upgrade to the pro version -- a one time cost of $10.99).

One thing I do is to plan my menu for the day the evening before or the morning of. I pre-enter all the foods and meals I intend to eat that day, and it shows me immediately whether I have planned for enough fat or too many carbs, or whether I might be able to afford a Keto treat if I want. If I don't eat something, I can delete it and sub in what I did eat instead.

Someone said this is a mysterious diet if you're not paying some guru a bazillion dollars to help you. NOT the slightest bit true. There are dozens and dozens of books and websites with "How Keto works" explanations, plus cooking and preparation blogs (showing you the fast track to planning and preparing for the week ahead if you have kids or are just a busy person). Plenty of YouTube videos.

I did Keto a couple of years ago, and it worked marvelously. But I got off of it because I was so bored. My doctor told me to have bullet-proof coffee, bacon and eggs for a late breakfast, and then a steak with 1 cup of greens for dinner. I got so I couldn't look at another steak or egg. The Stupid Simple Keto app helps keep you in line with your goals and makes it easy for you not to get bored because you don't have to follow such a restrictive diet when you have the means of keeping track of what you're eating.

I am very impressed with this app. I love puzzles of all kinds, and I am pretty good at them. But these are really challenging me. I particularly like that it is turn-taking and not timed. I need the time to think! I also really like that you can unlock three puzzles at a time if you get three stars. Totally recommended!

The screen shots do not do this app justice. I think there are 10 activities to complete. Jackman reads a couple of pages and then guides you to the next activity. They are simple enough that a preschooler will not be frustrated but engaging enough to hold interest. The directions are very clear, always good for small ones. You can go through the whole thing page by page, but you can also skip to the activity you want on a picture menu. Also, when all the badges are earned, you can clear them in the parent menu, and do it again. I really like that touch, especially because my kids are sharing. With gorgeous pictures and lots of interesting sounds, this is a lot like interacting with the show. No glitches on my Fire HD. I don't see any way this could be improved.

My only wish is that I could get more detailed pollen information. Still, I am happy to have this improved app.

I was stunned by how great this app is. I love this kind of puzzle, and this is the best I have ever seen it done. The controls are easy to use, and the navigation is simple. I found no glitches at all. But my favorite thing about this app is how challenging the puzzles themselves are. I have found that most of these apps are only pleasant distractions because they are fairly easy. Not this one! The normal levels takes some brain power, and the difficult levels take real work. This is my new favorite app, and I will be playing it for hours!

I really enjoyed the first Joining Hands, and this one is even better. They have made several improvements, my favorite being the hint button. I got really stuck on a couple in the first app, so I like knowing that won't happen again. The new characters are a fun addition, too. Wonderful app!

I had a great time playing this. The puzzles were very good. The type of puzzle varies so that some seem easy and some a true challenge. The puzzles are timed but not too harshly. I agree with other reviewers that the narrator is wonderful -- so funny. My favorite part is that you can go back to the puzzles you do not do so well on and get a gold medal later. That is a terrific feature. The graphics and characters are excellent. My only criticism is that a couple of puzzles near the end of the game did not work the first time on my one-year old Kindle Fire HD 7". I had to skip them and go back later to get them to work. Because I got them to work later, I did not dock a star. Anyway, this was enough fun that I would tolerate a messed-up puzzle to play the rest. Hope there are more of these coming!

Mainly because I beat it on my first game! That's biased me toward it but not unreasonably so. I am no chess player. I don't generally find it that exciting, preferring strategy games on the computer but a part of me feels I should at least understand it on a basic level.

Problem has always been finding a fairly matched opponent. It's sort of like going for a run with someone. To be enjoyable you need to be comfortable at roughly the same pace. This game so far has been that partner. I did win, but it wasn't a walk in the park. I was at the lowest level so I can move up levels if I want some losses.
The game itself, as in the mechanics of it, is great. The movement is easy, intuitive and forgiving (i.e., you can undo a move). When you press on a piece it shows you all the possible moves with dotted lines emanating out from the piece. Believe it or not, at least for me, this makes a difference in deciding on a move...it doesn't help with strategy, but on an individual move it is clarifying to see the possibilities. As far as strategy, I have none when it comes to chess. I just don't see it with the game; I know it's there because too many others do see it, but for me I never 'get it'. I'm hoping that with a good partner (Chess Free) I will begin to develop that sight for strategy with the game. Maybe I will, maybe I won't but at least I'll know over time now that I have a way to play while maintaining interest.

Why do these types of games so quickly devolve into an exercise in frustration? The difficulty curve comes not from clever level design, but rather by inserting obstacles that are near impossible to pass and are totally uninteresting to boot. The game should be called Trial and Error Extreme.

The production values are on par with games like Where's My Water, which is saying a lot. The game is very well produced, with sharp, charming graphics and fun, engaging puzzle gameplay. This is a good buy even if you miss it while it's the faotd.

This game has the potential to be truly awesome. Good graphics and lighting with solid run and gun control mechanics. However, I think some basic design choices really undermine the experience.

First, enemies infinitely respawn and do so way too quickly. It is literally impossible to clear an area even momentarily. Some may enjoy the frantic pace that this creates, but I do not.

This is made worse by the fact that this game employs the more contemporary "fast" zombies. Call me old-school, but I prefer my zombies slow and lumbering.

This, too, might be acceptable if the player was able to move a bit faster. Since when are zombies actually quicker on their feet than a normal person? There is a sprint button but it is virtually useless because it only lasts a couple of seconds and then has to recharge. By the time you've stopped shooting long enough to sprint away from a large group of zombies and then turned around to actually start shooting, they are right back on top of you. And in the meantime, a whole slew of new zombies are spawning behind you and you have to sprint away again.

Another minor complaint is the fact that you don't control the shooting at all. It just happens automatically whenever you are facing in the general direction of an enemy. It actually works pretty well most of the time, but other times you'll be pointlessly blasting away at a zombie on the other side of a truck bed, just wasting ammo.

Another issue is that the game provides very little direction to let you know where you're supposed to be going. I made it to the 7th or 8th level and quit out of frustration because I had absolutely no idea what I was supposed to be doing or where I was supposed to be going. There is little room for exploration as you are constantly battling against respawning zombies.

This is all compounded even further by the fact that your character can only take about 4 or 5 hits before dying. There are no checkpoints, so you'll be starting the level over each time you die. Fortunately, levels are pretty short so this isn't a huge problem.

At the very least, the game would benefit from having some choice of difficulty. Any easy mode where you can take about 3 times as many hits before dying would be enough to make the game less frustrating and more enjoyable.

If a friend had shown this to me without telling me what it was called, I would have assumed it was an official OutRun release. It's that good. If the goal was to create a nostalgic throwback to racing games of the late 80s and early 90s, then they've executed perfectly.  My only suggestions for improvement would be to add branching paths, like the original OutRun, and to separate the scoreboard to distinguish by course. Currently it appears that all scores go onto the same leaderboard whether you played course A or B. The controls are so spot on, I can't praise them enough. I'll be keeping this installed as it is perfect for a quick old-school fix.

It's not exactly a negative, but I found this game to be a lot more difficult than others in the genre. This was partly due to bugginess and partly due to the developer just making a harder game that doesn't hold your hand or have overly obvious solutions.

I admit I tried to use hints a couple of times and found them to be pretty useless, mostly just telling me what I already knew, or being so vague as to be more frustrating than helpful.

There's a really annoying tile puzzle section that I got stuck on for a while until I realized there was an option to skip buried in the settings menu. Thank god for that or I probably would not have had the patience to complete the game.

Finally, either the game has the most anticlimactic ending ever, or it glitched out when I solved the final puzzle. There was no cutscene or anything to wrap things up. It just sat there and I was stuck on that screen. Kind of a disappointing way to finish an otherwise enjoyable game. I don't feel inclined to play through the whole thing again just to find out.

The controls are awful (both touch and virtual stick). That's really my only complaint. Unfortunately, it's a big one and really kept me from enjoying the game. I'll check back when it's updated to see if they've tightened things up. The game seems pretty good otherwise, so here's to hoping...

I've used Quicken since it came out in the late 1980s. I've tried other products along the way and always come back to Quicken. I don't know what I'd do without my quicken.
When you first get started with the program, to take full advantage of it, it takes some setting up. How detailed you want to keep track of your expenses and bills is really up to you. For example. I have every transaction from every credit card and I've attached the receipts to each transaction. If I pay a bill with several areas of charges, like DWP, I actually separate my charges for water, power, sewer etc, all attached to the single credit card transaction. I can go back over years and tell you exactly how much I paid my kids doctors and for what. I also attach key codes for software I purchase so I always have them and manuals for my appliances. I even download copies of all my insurance policies and attach them to the payments so I can always go back and review my coverage; the pink slip to my car attached to the payment, contracts for work I have done.
I can also keep track of all my bills, when the closing dates are on my accounts and the due dates on all my bills. I don't need to get a bill in the mail to know when it should have arrived and when it's due. I can set links to the web sites of all the accounts I setup so that I can go to each web site and see just want the charges are and download them into the account. One of the best things is, I can back up all this information onto one flash drive and have everything I might need in an emergency.

Every so often I think about my resume and how out-of-date it is. I jot down a task to update it and then put it off because updating a resume is so much fun... And then it goes unmodified for years. So when I decided to really just get it done this time I found I had a lot of writer's block. I sought out sample resumes, blogs, and so on, but still couldn't quite get into the groove, so I purchased ResumeMaker on a whim.

If you have an existing resume it does a pretty good job of parsing yours into their format. Their format is extremely important and I'll touch on that later. It takes a section-by-section approach and allows you to add as many sections as you would like. It gives you guidance on "Action words" and "Sample phrases", the latter of which was most helpful as it jogged my memory a bit. You go through their editor to make changes, spellcheck, perform reviews, and then export into multiple formats, like PDF and Word.

It's a bit clunky to work with and the display of your resume gets a bit goofed up at times, but for someone that needs a bit of guidance, it works pretty well. I haven't gotten into any of the interviewing tips, job seeker tips, and such at this point.

I don't think it's a bad tool for creating a resume. If you are a bit more established in your resume skills and don't want an interface in front of your editing, then it's a bit of overhead you may not need. I mentioned their format earlier and they do have a proprietary format for your resume. From my experience I'll let you know that making changes to formatting outside of their wizard causes hardship when you export to other formats. The formatting gets messed up and you have to manually edit and reformat those exports - not something I care to do. I should also mention that they have 50 or so resume themes/formats that you can apply to your resume so you can pick the style that works best for you. Big time-saver.

Disappointed on this one. The idea was interesting, but the app doesn't work.

1. Pressing ENTER to advance to a new line causes the cursor to go upwards to a previous line. If you don't catch that, you wind up writing your new line in the middle of an old line.

2. Advancing to a new line has a habit highlighting/selecting a chuck of text earlier in the note. If you don't catch that you wind up overwriting previous text.

Example:
Here is the result of typing a paragraph of three sentences followed by one bulleted item:

"Everton knows g Joe Tripp3 d here is bullelist. .this"

Summing it up: there's no way you can use this as a note-taking program under these conditions. There are far too many options offering a far better experience.

If you do elect to use this one, keep in mind that there's no undo / redo, which is inconvenient. More importantly, there's no undo on a note deletion. Once you delete it, even if accidentally, it is gone - permanently. No backups can be made.

I'd give this one a single star if it wasn't for the novel idea of capturing random notes.

Not recommended...

I was looking for an alternative to Quickbooks and was offer a free trial of Sage 50 Premium. At first glance, while expensive at almost $600 it looked to be a full featured and easy to use small business accounting software program. I won't go into all the features, you can read the description to get that information. However, in small print you will discover that Sage is a money grab. Even after spending $600, they will REQUIRE a paid support plan and that you keep the software updated to be able to use it. Should you cancel your support plan, you will only have read only access to your data. This is absurd. Quickbooks is 1/3 the price and while they would like you to keep current, you can use the program without spending another cent. I would stay away from this before you get sucked into a very expensive accounting system that will be difficult and costly to migrate to another program when you do finally realize how insanely expensive this will be. Here is the fine print:

Minimum one-year commitment required. Valid credit card and Internet access required to activate and maintain support and services. To ensure continuous service, your Sage Business Care plan is an automatically renewing plan, and you will be charged up to a week prior to your renewal date. The subscription plan is an annual subscription with a lease to the software license; therefore, you can only use the software while you are on the plan. You may terminate your subscription plan with thirty (30) days’ advance notice to Sage and receive a pro-rated refund. However, if you terminate your subscription plan or if your subscription payment is not received, you will have read-only access to your data, and full program functionality will not be restored until you have brought your account current. The subscription plan requires that you be on the most current version of the software to continue your subscription.

I have been using TurboTax for many many years. I have seen the product get better over the years. They have changed the features in the different editions so be sure the version has the features that you need. They have done this to make you buy an upgrade and have expanded their opportunities to monetize the software over the years. I certainly do not fault them but just be careful in selecting your version and be aware of the filing charges as well as State program fees. Many of these options are available for free if you look elsewhere. With TurboTax you pay for convenience.  As far as the program itself, it is complete and easy to use. Definitely makes tax filing a breeze even with being self employed and having to file K-1's as well as various other form of 1099 income. It has never let me down.

I have a love/hate relationship with Quickbooks. I'be been using Quickbooks for over 25 years, and continue to do so. Why? Because it works, it's versitle and inexpensive. I've used it in a manufacturing business with over 5,000 inventory items, a construction company that had not only inventory items but mostly custom items, and several other small businesses to track payables, receivables, reconcile bank accounts, prepare estimates and most of all, generate reports of an infinite varier=ty. The one thing that I never used was the payroll function. I feel it's still better to use a 3rd party like ADP or Paychex for that. It's easier and they handle all the complexities and required filings. P/R is a pain in the butt and is better left to then experts. That's the love part. What I don't like, the hate part, is the way they have complicated the program without providing documentation and continue to monetize every aspect they can of the program. Want support? pay up. Want tutorials? pay up. Want payroll? pay up. It seems that over the years more and more windows pop up that try to sell you something. I feel bad for those just jumping on the Quickbooks train now, it's going to be a steep learning curve and you'll undoubtedly be reaching into your wallet more. When I first started, it was super easy to use, you paid for the software and that was it. The manual was extensive and you were on your way. Over the years, that changed. It seems be be the way Intuit runs their business as the same applies to TurboTax with regard to monetizing features. In any event, it's a great package that will handle the needs of most small businesses with easy. It's considerably less expensive than Sage and some of the others that are not as polished. So, putting the hate part of my relationship aside, I can, and often do reccomend Quickbooks to anyone looking for small business accounting software.

This is the best file manager/explorer I've used on android devices.  I tried a lot of different file managers, but this one just does everything a little slicker and better. This is a very interesting game based on Mahjong, where you work through increasingly difficult levels.  While not conventional Mahjong, it implements all of the classic rules well and is a great diversion.  The most difficult levels are very challenging.  A good job by the developers and I recommend it.

This is a not very interesting and unconventional game only loosely based on classic Mahjong. In this "free" version you can ony play through the first extremely simple seven levels.  At that point they want you to signup for a monthly recurring fee in order to play "forever". They make a pitch about "community play", but really mean "community pay". The game is much too simplified, with no more challenge than tic-tac-toe. I would avoid this one like the plague.
This puzzle game looks simple, and in concept it is, but in practice, as you go higher in difficulty, it gets very challenging.  Great game, implemented  very well.  Love it!

If you really want to know how your device performs and compares to others, this is the app.  There are a lot of benchmark apps out there and some of them very good.  PassMark has long been an industry standard for performance measurement on PCs, Disk Drives, Video Cards, etc.  Now that same high standard of measurement has been adapted to mobile devices.  If you really want to see how your device stacks up, try this one.

This is a nice little app, but it definitely is not universal, since it doesn't comvert many different types of measures, such as area, force, etc. A well-crafted app, but of somewhat limited use to me as is.
This app will show you everything you need to know to keep your battery performing at peak.  It will manage the charging cycles and battery usage if you set it up correctly.  A good solid app.

This app provides clear and easy to read information about your wi-fi connection(s).  If you are haveing problems with dropped connections, etc., this can help you find the problem and fix it.  It does not fix anything for you, but does provide the information you need to do so.  A very useful app for me.

This is a really interesting implementation with a floating, rotating board and really nice graphics.  It is missing any means of initiating a reshuffle, however.  If not for that it would definitely get 5 stars.  It is very challenging, since perspective comes in to play when trying to match tiles.  I play this version a fair amount, but it is not my favorite.  Still, a good, if incomplete, effort.

This looked like it would be a fun game, but unfortunately turned into a waste of time and I just uninstalled it from my Kindle Fire.  I found the puzzles (the handful that I actually did) to be extremely hard in some places and then super-easy in others. To make things even more annoying, I kept being asked what seemed like every minute if I liked the game and to go rate it! And then of course I barely got past a couple of scenes and I'm being asked to pay to unlock it further. No thanks.

There are a few bugs where I found myself pounding the screen to make something happen (played on Kindle Fire), so I should have quit sooner, but I'm one of those people who has to finish what I start. The story was horrible, and in a nutshell: {Spoiler alert! sort of} woman goes to Paris, takes 1 art class, suddenly falls in love with another student vampire, go back & forth around Paris, then they run away together. The games are short and seemed thrown together and didn't make sense.

A lot of things were ridiculous filler and a waste of time (eg. objects or people light up/glow & tell you to click on it - like "talk to John Smith" then it starts the script) and other games started timing you all of a sudden (huh?). Didn't pay much for it, but still a waste...

I like that there are tons of variations on this game but slightly frustrated that you cant pick more than 7 items each round.  overall would recommend.

The playing-card puzzles in between scenes did get tiresome and there were times when I struggled to pick up a specific card and it kept restarting the game (annoying when you have 20 cards to keep starting over). The title is basically what it's about (going around the world and doing puzzles in various destinations) and the story and graphics were ok. Overall not the worst game out there, but nothing special that deserves to be more than .99 cents.

If, on the other hand, the app's true purpose is data farming or worse, then obviously they would be against full disclosure.
From now on, explain the permissions! If you agree with me, then help me get this message out. If not, tell me why.

The game lives up to its name. You can play as various characters and take on different quests, crawling through randomly-generated dungeons, killing everything and collecting loot. Sounds simple, right? And that's all it really is, at its core. It's a mobile game meant to be picked up and played for short periods of time, such as on your train commute home from class. You can't really expect an epic adventure on a mobile game unless it's a port like Dragon Quest VIII or Final Fantasy Dimensions (both of which I recommend, by the way). I kind of lost interest in it fairly quickly, to be honest. And the main reason for that is that the controls and the visuals. The graphics, while intentionally pixellated, are horribly so. There isn't much detail to be able to discern much without squinting at the screen, the text is barely readable, and the menu buttons are so small I can not only not figure out what they are, I can barely tap them. The controls took a few minutes to figure out, and even longer to realize that, yes, I could ZOOM IN! But that still didn't fix the interface issues. I think this really WAS meant for tablets like the Kindle Fire, though one reviewer said even on a 7" Fire HDX, the text was still unreadable. I wouldn't recommend this game.

I'm quite impressed with this product and may purchase it again in the future if the price is right when my subscription runs out. I really liked the fact it gave two years instead of one, so I don't have to worry about it as often and also that it is for up to three PCs. The software doesn't hassle you much, runs without a huge system performance hit (you can select lesser protection levels if you need to reduce the performance hit even further), and in general it has worked really well for me. I've had no damage from viruses since getting this software, though I generally have almost none.

You should be aware though, this is not a full suite. It's an anti-virus program only, so no firewall. I actually like that better as I've handled my firewall with separate software anyway. For me it was just one less thing to turn off. I also like that the updates seem to come more frequently than they did with Norton. From the reviews I've read, BitDefender has a very good detection record and I like it much better than Norton. I can't think of any reason not to suggest this suite.

I've been using TurboTax for quite a few years now, really since I started paying any real taxes. The first thing I noticed is TurboTax 2009 is much slower and buggier than 2008. I had no problems telling the program to update only when I told it to, which is a must for me. I despise automatic updates in almost everything except my browser; I've had far too many experiences where an automatic update got in the way of what I was trying to do. Anyway, the updating failed twice. I had to kill the program and reboot. On the third try, the update succeeded, but ran very slowly. Since then, updates have been pretty much normal, but the program takes noticeably longer to open up than 2008 did. Nothing gives me reason to think it will mess up on tax calculations, but the program feels lower quality than last year's offering. I keep a couple copies of my save files around though, just in case I corrupt one. Better safe than sorry.

One nice thing, 2009 seems to do a better job than 2008 in making it easy to stop and start entering your information if you can't do it all at one time. I entered my W2 information, then tried to download the data instead. When that download failed and I went back to manual, the stuff I'd started on was still there. Very cool. It is also pretty good about starting up right where you left off when you load a save and has helpful reminders if you filled in 2008 income sources but haven't updated those same values for 2009. The program handles everything from your basic W2, to mortgage related forms, interest income, stock dividends, and basically anything up to what most normal home owners (without complex stock holdings) would need.

When it works, I'm quite pleased with TurboTax. The steps it takes you through make things as painless as they can be given we live in a country where they make it such a complicated system that you have to pay someone to figure out how much you even owe the government. It can't help you when you're looking at that that nice big Federal tax liability on your W2 form and realize according to CNNMoney (October, 2009) an estimated 47% of American households will pay no federal income tax. That'll just frost your pumpkin.

I've been using BitDefender for the past couple of years. I found the 2008 version for 3 computers for two years at a great price. When it was running out, I went looking for a similar deal and found one.

I noticed a couple of unpolished elements when installing. There were a lot of DOS command prompt windows opening in the background on the screen very briefly. I didn't have to interact with any of them and they went away almost immediately so there's no harm to it. It's just a little unpolished.

I should also mention that the update for it is big. It will ask to download the updated installer, then after a few minutes when that's downloaded and run the updates for the program are currently over 75 MB. I think that's probably the case with many anti-virus programs, but just be aware if you're on dial-up you'll be downloading for quite some time.

I uninstalled that old [[ASIN:B000V809KW 2008 version]] from a laptop and a desktop. The desktop went fine, but the laptop failed to uninstall. I tried to get the uninstall program off Bitdefender's website, but the link they pointed to was dead. Eventually, I found the CD and reinstalled, which failed, but the CD had the uninstaller which worked. I only mention this because it's a little worrisome that if the last program had those issues that this version might when I eventually uninstall it.

I like this version of the program. It has several different modes ranging from Novice (hides settings) to expert (showing all of it) and is very easy to change between them. My absolute favorite part though, is the "you're not fully protected" system. In past programs I've used, if you disable some feature you constantly get the little alert icon that you're "at risk". Bitdefender 2010 lets you choose which of those things it monitors for. So I didn't want the anti-spam because I only use web mail, so I told it not to bother me that I'd deleted it. It may be a small thing, but to me it's a huge annoyance saver.

So far, I cannot tell if the scanner is faster or not. It scans at only about a quarter of the number of files per second as the old program, but it supposedly has an intelligent monitoring system which lets it avoid rescanning files that haven't changed and thus couldn't have picked up an infection. So while it wasn't that fast on the first scan, in theory it'll only get faster moving forward. It intentionally skipped thousands of files.

Default is a daily scan, which in my opinion is complete overkill. Unless you have a kid in your house, if the resident protection is running all the time you can get by with once or twice a week. Thankfully, the scheduling is very easy and you can even set the scans to take low priority, which is a nice touch.

In terms of detection, BitDefender isn't the highest rated scanner, but it's far from the lowest. It's an excellent budget anti-virus package and more than adequate for most people's needs. Considering how reasonable the pricing is, I'd happily recommend. However, since I've only used it a week or so, if it does do anything really weird I'll update my review to mention it.

It's put out by PC Tools and you can find it on CNET.

They've really pared back the installation package options. There are far fewer clicks. In general there are fewer options to customize it seems. One of the most startling changes is the lack of ability his schedule stands anymore. You can still start a manual scan, but in theory the program is scanning your system constantly when resources are available negating the need for a separate scan.
